body.objective: Students will be able to analyze art about identity.
body.iCan: I can analyze art about identity.
successCriteria: I can identify how artists show identity in their work
I can interpret symbols, colour and setting in a portrait
I can plan ideas for my own identity artwork
body.hook: A self-portrait can show much more than a face. Artists include objects, colours, backgrounds and symbols to show where they come from, what they care about and how they see themselves. Before you make art about identity, you'll learn to read how other artists do it.

vocabulary.definition: The qualities, beliefs, culture and experiences that make a person who they are.
An image or object that stands for an idea.

study.title: Reading Identity
study.question: How do artists express who they are?
study.passage:
Part 1, Gallery walk (15 minutes): Look at four portraits or self-portraits (shown from gallery websites), such as:
• A self-portrait with objects from the artist's daily life in the background.
• A portrait using bright, symbolic colours rather than realistic skin tones.
• A work by an Indigenous artist that combines a person with patterns, animals or land.
• A photo-collage portrait built from many images.
For each, record: What objects or symbols appear? What do colours suggest? What does the setting tell us? What might the artist want us to know?
Part 2, Identity web (10 minutes): Draw a web with your name in the middle. Add branches for family and culture, places, interests, values, challenges and goals.
Part 3, Symbol sketches (20 minutes): Choose three branches and sketch a symbol for each. For example: a mountain for growing up in Alberta, a basketball for a passion, a tree for family roots.
Privacy note: You choose what to share. Your identity artwork can show as much or as little as you're comfortable with.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; teachers show images from public gallery and museum websites.
steps: Share one symbol and its meaning with a partner
discussion: Which artwork told you the most about the artist? How?
Why might an artist use symbols instead of words?
Which of your symbols is strongest, and why?
study.product: Write a plan for an identity artwork: list three symbols, explain what each means, describe your colour choices and sketch a possible composition.

examples.title: Visual metaphor
examples.problem: Show "growing up" as a visual metaphor.
examples.answer: A sprouting plant or a tree with rings
examples.explore: Think of another metaphor for change.

body.objective: Students will be able to examine art as social commentary.
body.iCan: I can examine art as social commentary.
successCriteria: I can explain what social commentary in art is
I can analyze how an artwork communicates a message about society
I can evaluate how effective an artwork's message is
body.hook: Art doesn't only decorate walls; sometimes it argues. Picasso's Guernica protested the bombing of a town. Street artists paint messages about war, money and the environment on city walls. When art comments on society, it asks viewers to think, and sometimes to act.

vocabulary.definition: Art that expresses an opinion about society or an issue.
A topic people disagree about or want to change, such as war, poverty or the environment.
Art made to oppose something or call for change.
Placing contrasting things side by side to create meaning.
Using humour or exaggeration to criticize something.
How viewers react to an artwork's message.

study.title: Art With a Message
study.question: How does art comment on society?
study.passage:
Artworks to analyze (show images from public museum sources):
A. Pablo Picasso, Guernica (1937): a huge black, white and grey painting made after the bombing of the Spanish town of Guernica during the Spanish Civil War. Twisted figures, a screaming horse, a mother holding a child.
B. Brian Jungen (Dane-zaa and Swiss-Canadian), Prototype for New Understanding series (1998–2005): Nike Air Jordan sneakers cut apart and sewn into forms that look like Northwest Coast masks, raising questions about consumerism, sports culture and how Indigenous art is bought and sold.
C. Kent Monkman (Cree), large paintings that place his gender-fluid alter ego, Miss Chief Eagle Testickle, into scenes copied from famous colonial-era paintings, retelling history from an Indigenous point of view.
Task: Choose one work. Identify the issue, the message, the techniques used (colour, juxtaposition, scale, satire, symbols) and the intended audience. Then evaluate: is the message clear and powerful?
study.source: Summaries written for this lesson; teachers show images from public museum websites.
steps: Evaluate how effective the message is
discussion: What issue does the artwork address?
Which technique makes the message strongest?
Why might the artist have chosen this medium or scale?
Does art change people's minds? Give an example.
study.product: Write an analysis of one social commentary artwork: issue, message, techniques, audience and your evaluation with evidence.

examples.answer: Mass-produced sneakers and the form of traditional masks
examples.explore: What does that make viewers question?

examples.title: Retelling history
examples.problem: Why does Kent Monkman copy colonial-era paintings?
examples.answer: To retell history from an Indigenous perspective and challenge the original story

examples.title: Evaluating
examples.answer: "Guernica's screaming figures make the suffering of war impossible to ignore"

body.objective: Students will be able to research a Canadian artist.
body.iCan: I can research a Canadian artist.
successCriteria: I can research a Canadian artist using reliable sources
I can explain how the artist's life and context shaped their work
I can present my research clearly
body.hook: Canada has produced artists whose work changed how the world sees this land: Emily Carr's forests, the Group of Seven's rocky north, Daphne Odjig's flowing figures, Kenojuak Ashevak's owls. Today you become the expert on one of them.

vocabulary.definition: Finding and recording information to answer questions.
A trustworthy source, such as a gallery, museum or encyclopedia website.
The story of a person's life.
Something that affects an artist's style or ideas.
The features that make an artist's work recognizable.
A note telling where information came from.

study.title: Canadian Artist Study
study.question: How do an artist's life and context shape their art?
study.passage:
Research guide (written for this lesson):
Choose one artist: Emily Carr (1871–1945), Lawren Harris of the Group of Seven (1885–1970), Daphne Odjig (Odawa-Potawatomi, 1919–2016), Kenojuak Ashevak (Inuit, 1927–2013), Alex Janvier (Denesuline and Saulteaux, born 1935), Norval Morrisseau (Anishinaabe, 1932–2007), Mary Pratt (1935–2018) or Brian Jungen (born 1970).
Research questions: 1. When and where did they live? 2. What experiences shaped them? 3. What is their signature style (subjects, colours, techniques)? 4. What influenced them, and whom did they influence? 5. What is one important artwork, and what does it mean?
Sources: use the National Gallery of Canada, the Canadian Encyclopedia, the Art Canada Institute and gallery websites. Record a citation for each fact.
Product: a one-page artist profile with an image description, plus a small study (sketch or painting) in the artist's style, not a copy.
study.source: Research guide written for this lesson; students use public, reliable art-history websites.
steps: Make a small study in the artist's style
discussion: How did the artist's life shape their art?
What surprised you in your research?
How is your study in their style different from a copy?
study.product: Create a one-page artist profile with citations and a small original study inspired by the artist's style.

examples.title: Reliable sources
examples.problem: Is a random social-media post reliable?
steps: Who wrote it? Can it be checked?
examples.answer: Usually not; use galleries, museums or encyclopedias

examples.title: Context
examples.problem: How did northern Ontario shape the Group of Seven?
examples.answer: They painted rugged landscapes to create a distinct Canadian style in the early 1900s

examples.title: Signature style
examples.answer: Bold black outlines, bright colours and lines connecting figures (Woodland style)

examples.title: Study vs copy
examples.problem: What makes a study "in the style of" rather than a copy?
examples.answer: You use the artist's techniques on your own subject
